slides.title: What counts as evidence of bias?

transcription.tex: I throw a coin 10 times. For what numbers of heads might you conclude that the coin is biased towards heads? Why?

shapes.alt: Binomial distribution for ten independent fair-coin tosses. Nine and ten heads are shaded. Their combined probability is 11/1024.

transcription.tex: Under the fair-coin model, $X\sim B(10,0.5)$. The expected number of heads is 5.\par A bias towards heads would make unusually large counts evidence against that model.
$P(X\ge8)=56/1024\approx0.0547$.\par $P(X\ge9)=11/1024\approx0.0107$.\par At the 5% level, 9 or 10 heads provide sufficient evidence. Eight heads fall just below the rejection threshold.
A hypothesis is a statement about a population parameter. A test uses sample evidence to decide whether to reject the null hypothesis $H_0$ in favour of the alternative $H_1$.
I throw a coin 10 times. For what numbers of heads might you conclude that the coin is biased towards heads? Why?
Let $p$ be the probability of heads and $X$ the number of heads in ten independent tosses. Under the fair-coin model, $X\sim\mathrm{B}(10,0.5)$.
$H_0:p=0.5$. The coin is fair.
$H_1:p>0.5$. A bias towards heads would make large counts more likely.

shapes.alt: Under a fair coin, five heads is most likely. The two small upper-tail bars for nine and ten heads are shaded red.

transcription.tex: For a 5% upper-tail test, $P(X\ge8)=0.0547$ and $P(X\ge9)=0.0107$. With 9 or 10 heads, reject $H_0$. With 0 to 8 heads there is insufficient evidence of a bias towards heads.

transcription.tex: Let \(X\) be the number of heads in ten independent tosses. Before observing the tosses, \(X\) is a random variable. Its possible values are the integers from 0 to 10.
After the tosses, the observed count is a number. For example, nine heads gives \(x=9\). We use the count \(X\) as our test statistic.
If each toss has probability \(p\) of heads, then \(X\sim\mathrm B(10,p)\). Under the null hypothesis \(p=0.5\), the graph gives the probability of each possible count.
For a bias towards heads, the evidence is the probability of the observed count or a more extreme count under \(H_0\). For nine heads, add the two shaded bars: \(P(X\ge9)=11/1024\).

transcription.tex: The significance level \(\alpha\) sets an upper bound on the probability of rejecting \(H_0\) when it is true. Common choices are 5% and 1%. Choose the level before seeing the data.
For a 5% test against a bias towards heads, start at the right-hand end of the graph. Include large counts while keeping their combined probability at most 0.05 under \(H_0\).
\(P(X\ge9)=(10+1)/1024\approx0.0107\), whereas \(P(X\ge8)=(45+10+1)/1024\approx0.0547\). Including eight heads would exceed 5%.
The critical region is \(\{9,10\}\). Reject the fair-coin hypothesis for nine or ten heads. For fewer heads the evidence is insufficient. The actual probability of a false rejection is about 1.07%.
How can ten coin tosses provide evidence about the chance of heads?

shapes.alt: A front view of a coin marked Heads.

transcription.tex: Write $p$ for the probability of heads. Test $H_0:p=0.5$ against $H_1:p>0.5$.\par The alternative determines which tail to use.
Count the heads in ten independent tosses. Under $H_0$, $X\sim B(10,0.5)$.\par For an observed count $x$, calculate $P(X\ge x)$ under the null model.

If that upper-tail probability is at most the chosen significance level, reject the fair-coin hypothesis and report evidence of bias towards heads. Otherwise the sample gives insufficient evidence of such a bias.
John wants to see whether a coin is unbiased or whether it is biased towards coming down heads. He tosses the coin 8 times and counts the number of times X, it lands head uppermost.
Both hypotheses concern the population parameter \(p\), the probability of heads on a single toss.
\(H_0:p=0.5\). Under the null hypothesis the coin is fair. Each toss has probability \(0.5\) of coming down heads.
\(H_1:p>0.5\). John is specifically testing for a bias towards heads. Large counts of heads provide evidence in this direction.

A directional alternative such as \(p>0.5\) uses the upper tail. A bias towards tails, \(p<0.5\), would use the lower tail. To test for bias in either direction, use \(H_1:p\ne0.5\) and consider both tails.

transcription.tex: Question 1
(a) Explain what you understand by a hypothesis test. \par (b) Define a null hypothesis and an alternative hypothesis and state the symbols used for each. \par (c) Define a test statistic.
(a) A hypothesis is a statement about a population parameter. A test uses a sample or experiment to decide whether to reject that statement.
(b) $H_0$ is the assumption being tested. $H_1$ describes the alternative value or range of the parameter.
(c) A statistic calculated from the sample or experiment and used to test the hypothesis.
Question 2

For each of these hypotheses, state whether the hypotheses given describe a one-tailed or a two-tailed test.\par (a) \(H_0:p=0.8,\ H_1:p>0.8\)\par (b) \(H_0:p=0.6,\ H_1:p\ne0.6\)\par (c) \(H_0:p=0.2,\ H_1:p<0.2\).
(a) One-tailed (upper).
(b) Two-tailed.
(c) One-tailed (lower).
Question 3

Dmitri wants to see whether a dice is biased towards the value 6. He throws the dice 60 times and counts the number of sixes he gets. \par (a) Describe the test statistic. \par (b) Write down a suitable null hypothesis to test this dice. \par (c) Write down a suitable alternative hypothesis to test this dice.
(a) Number of sixes in 60 rolls.
(b) $H_0:p=\tfrac16$, where $p$ is the probability of a six.
(c) $H_1:p>\tfrac16$.
Question 4

Shell wants to test to see whether a coin is biased. She tosses the coin 100 times and counts the number of times she gets a head. Shell says that her test statistic is the probability of the coin landing on heads. \par (a) Explain the mistake that Shell has made and state the correct test statistic for her test. \par (b) Write down a suitable null hypothesis to test this coin. \par (c) Write down a suitable alternative hypothesis to test this coin.
(a) The probability of heads is the parameter. The statistic is the observed number of heads in 100 tosses.
(b) $H_0:p=\tfrac12$.
(c) $H_1:p\ne\tfrac12$.
Question 5

In a manufacturing process the proportion (p) of faulty articles has been found, from long experience, to be 0.1. A sample of 100 articles from a new manufacturing process is tested, and 8 are found to be faulty. The manufacturers wish to test at the 5% level of significance whether or not there has been a reduction in the proportion of faulty articles. \par (a) Suggest a suitable test statistic. \par (b) Write down two suitable hypotheses. \par (c) Explain the condition under which the null hypothesis is rejected.
(a) Number of faulty articles among the 100.
(c) Reject $H_0$ if $P(X\le8)$ under $H_0$ is at most 0.05.

transcription.tex: Question 2
A test statistic has a distribution \(B(10,p)\). Given that \(H_0:p=0.2\), \(H_1:p>0.2\), find the critical region for the test using a 5% significance level.
Question 3
A random variable has a distribution \(B(20,p)\). A single observation is used to test \(H_0:p=0.15\) against \(H_1:p<0.15\). Using a 5% level of significance, find the critical region of this test.
Under $H_0$, $X\sim B(20,0.15)$.\par $P(X\le1)=0.1756>0.05$ but $P(X=0)=0.0388<0.05$.\par Critical value 0; region $X=0$.
Question 4

A random variable has distribution \(B(20,p)\). A single observation is used to test \(H_0:p=0.4\) against \(H_1:p\ne 0.4\). \par (a) Using the 5% level of significance, find the critical region of this test. \par (b) Write down the actual significance level of the test.
Question 5
A test statistic has a distribution \(B(20,p)\). Given that \(H_0:p=0.18\), \(H_1:p<0.18\), find the critical region for the test using a 1% level of significance.
Under $H_0$, $X\sim B(20,0.18)$.\par $P(X=0)=0.82^{20}=0.0189>0.01$.\par Even the smallest observation exceeds the 1% tail probability. The lower critical region is empty.
Question 6

A random variable has distribution \(B(10,p)\). A single observation is used to test \(H_0:p=0.22\) against \(H_1:p\ne 0.22\). \par (a) Using a 1% level of significance, find the critical region of this test. The probability in each tail should be as close as possible to 0.005. \par (b) Write down the actual significance level of the test.

(a) Under $H_0$, $X\sim B(10,0.22)$.\par $P(X=0)=0.0834$, so use an empty lower tail.\par $P(X\ge6)=0.01039$ and $P(X\ge7)=0.001580$. The latter is closer to 0.005.\par The critical region is $X\ge7$.
(b) Actual significance level: $0.001580\times100\%=0.158\%$.
Question 7

A mechanical component fails, on average, 3 times out of every 10. An engineer designs a new system of manufacture that he believes reduces the likelihood of failure. He tests a sample of 20 components made using his new system. \par (a) Describe the test statistic. \par (b) State suitable null and alternative hypotheses. \par (c) Using a 5% level of significance, find the critical region for a test to check his belief, ensuring the probability is as close as possible to 0.05. \par (d) Write down the actual significance level of the test.
(a) Number of failed components.
(c) Under $H_0$, $X\sim B(20,0.3)$.\par $P(X\le2)=0.0355$ and $P(X\le3)=0.1071$. The closer value is 0.0355. Region: $X\le2$.
Question 8

Seedlings come in trays of 36. On average, 12 seedlings survive to be planted on. A gardener decides to use a new fertiliser on the seedlings which she believes will improve the number that survive. \par (a) Describe the test statistic and state suitable null and alternative hypotheses. \par (b) Using a 10% level of significance, find the critical region for a test to check her belief. \par (c) State the probability of incorrectly rejecting \(H_0\) using this critical region.
(a) $X$ counts surviving seedlings. $H_0:p=1/3$, $H_1:p>1/3$.
Question 9

A restaurant owner notices that her customers typically choose lasagne one fifth of the time. She changes the recipe and believes this will change the proportion of customers choosing lasagne. \par (a) Suggest a model and state suitable null and alternative hypotheses. She takes a random sample of 25 customers. \par (b) Find, at the 5% level of significance, the critical region for a test to check her belief. \par (c) State the probability of incorrectly rejecting \(H_0\).
(a) $X$ counts customers choosing lasagne. $X\sim B(25,p)$; $H_0:p=0.2$, $H_1:p\ne0.2$.

(b) Under $H_0$, $X\sim B(25,0.2)$. Compare with 0.025 per tail.\par $P(X=0)=0.0038$; $P(X\le1)=0.0274$, closer to 0.025.\par $P(X\ge9)=0.0468$; $P(X\ge10)=0.0173$, closer to 0.025.\par Region: $X\le1$ or $X\ge10$.

transcription.tex: The standard treatment for a particular disease has a $\frac25$ probability of success. A certain doctor has undertaken research in this area and has produced a new drug which has been successful with 11 out of 20 patients. The doctor claims the new drug represents an improvement on the standard treatment.\par Test, at the 5% significance level, the claim made by the doctor.

Let $p$ be the probability of success for a patient receiving the new drug. Let $X$ count the successes in 20 independent treatments, so $X\sim B(20,p)$.\par Test $H_0:p=0.4$ against $H_1:p>0.4$.\par Under $H_0$, $X\sim B(20,0.4)$. The observed count is 11. Use the upper tail because the claimed change is an improvement.\par $P(X\ge11)=1-P(X\le10)\approx0.1275$.\par $0.1275>0.05$, so we do not reject $H_0$. The results give insufficient evidence at the 5% level that the new drug improves the success rate.

transcription.tex: Question 1

A single observation, x, is taken from a binomial distribution \(B(10,p)\) and a value of 5 is obtained. Use this observation to test \(H_0:p=0.25\) against \(H_1:p>0.25\) using a 5% significance level.
$H_0:p=0.25,\ H_1:p>0.25$. Under $H_0$, $X\sim B(10,0.25)$.\par $P(X\ge5)=1-P(X\le4)=0.0781>0.05$.\par Do not reject $H_0$. There is insufficient evidence for $p>0.25$.
Question 2
A random variable has distribution \(X\sim B(10,p)\). A single observation of x = 1 is taken from this distribution. Test, at the 5% significance level, \(H_0:p=0.4\) against \(H_1:p<0.4\).
$H_0:p=0.4,\ H_1:p<0.4$. Under $H_0$, $X\sim B(10,0.4)$.\par $P(X\le1)=0.0464<0.05$.\par Reject $H_0$. There is sufficient evidence for $p<0.4$.
Question 3

A single observation, x, is taken from a binomial distribution \(B(20,p)\) and a value of 10 is obtained. Use this observation to test \(H_0:p=0.3\) against \(H_1:p>0.3\) using a 5% significance level.
$H_0:p=0.3,\ H_1:p>0.3$. Under $H_0$, $X\sim B(20,0.3)$.\par $P(X\ge10)=1-P(X\le9)=0.0480<0.05$.\par Reject $H_0$. There is sufficient evidence for $p>0.3$.
Question 4

$H_0:p=0.45,\ H_1:p<0.45$. Under $H_0$, $X\sim B(20,0.45)$.\par $P(X\le3)=0.0049<0.01$.\par Reject $H_0$. There is sufficient evidence for $p<0.45$.
Question 5

A single observation, x, is taken from a binomial distribution \(B(20,p)\) and a value of 2 is obtained. Use this observation to test \(H_0:p=0.28\) against \(H_1:p<0.28\) using a 5% significance level.
$H_0:p=0.28,\ H_1:p<0.28$. Under $H_0$, $X\sim B(20,0.28)$.\par $P(X\le2)=0.0526>0.05$.\par Do not reject $H_0$. There is insufficient evidence for $p<0.28$.
Question 6
A random variable has distribution \(X\sim B(8,p)\). A single observation of x = 7 is taken from this distribution. Test, at the 5% significance level, \(H_0:p=0.32\) against \(H_1:p>0.32\).
$H_0:p=0.32,\ H_1:p>0.32$. Under $H_0$, $X\sim B(8,0.32)$.\par $P(X\ge7)=1-P(X\le6)=0.0020<0.05$.\par Reject $H_0$. There is sufficient evidence for $p>0.32$.
Question 7

A dice used in playing a board game is suspected of not giving the number 6 often enough. During a particular game it was rolled 12 times and only one 6 appeared. Does this represent significant evidence, at the 5% level of significance, that the probability of a 6 on this dice is less than \(\frac16\)?
$H_0:p=\tfrac16,\ H_1:p<\tfrac16$. Under $H_0$, $X\sim B(12,\tfrac16)$.\par $P(X\le1)=0.3813>0.05$.\par Do not reject $H_0$. Insufficient evidence that a six is less likely than one sixth.
Question 8

The success rate of the standard treatment for patients suffering from a particular skin disease is claimed to be 68%. \par (a) In a sample of n patients, X is the number for which the treatment is successful. Write down a suitable distribution to model X. Give reasons for your choice of model. A random sample of 10 patients receives the standard treatment and in only 3 cases was the treatment successful. It is thought that the standard treatment was not as effective as it is claimed. \par (b) Test the claim at the 5% level of significance.
(a) $X\sim B(n,0.68)$: fixed $n$, two outcomes, independent patients and constant probability of success.
(b) $H_0:p=0.68,\ H_1:p<0.68$. Under $H_0$, $X\sim B(10,0.68)$.\par $P(X\le3)=0.0155<0.05$.\par Reject $H_0$. There is evidence that the treatment is less effective than claimed.
